title: Interpreting Willingness-to-Pay for Workplace Attributes: Preferences or Constraints?
speaker: Basit Zafar (University of Michigan)
description:
Title:
Interpreting Willingness-to-Pay for Workplace Attributes: Preferences or Constraints? (with Yuting Chen, Patricia Cortes, Gizem Kosar, and Jessica Pan)
Abstract:
A large literature interprets differences in willingness to pay (WTP) for non-wage job attributes as reflecting differences in preferences. We show that measured WTP may also reflect differences in the constraints workers face. We study this using a two-wave panel survey in which the same respondents evaluate the same hypothetical jobs in 2020 and 2023, together with a within-person survey experiment that varies childcare availability while holding the job offers fixed. Consistent with the cross-sectional literature, we first show that women have a higher WTP than men for remote work, scheduling flexibility, and part-time work, with these differences concentrated among parents. These gender differences, however, may reflect differences in preferences, constraints, or both. To shed light on the role of constraints, we leverage the relaxation of childcare constraints between 2020 and 2023. As these constraints eased, we find that WTP for flexibility declined among mothers of young children, with no comparable declines among fathers or non-parents. While these patterns are consistent with constraints shaping measured WTP, changes over time may also reflect changes in preferences. We then turn to our survey experiment, which exogenously changes only the childcare constraint. Experimentally tightening childcare constraints increases mothers' WTP for all three flexibility attributes, while WTPs for other job attributes are largely unchanged. The differential responses of women and men to the experimental constraint are equivalent to 29--52 percent of the corresponding gender gaps in WTP. Taken together, our findings show that differences in measured WTP need not reflect differences in preferences alone: constraints can account for an economically meaningful part of these differences. This distinction matters for both the interpretation of WTP estimates and policy.

title: Personal Platforms and Community Design: The Influencer Markets
speaker: Maria Rosa Battaggion (University of Bergamo)
description:
Title:
Personal Platforms and Community Design: The Influencer Markets
Abstract:
We show that influencers constitute a previously unrecognized class of platform, with distinctive features that cannot be reduced to those of conventional platforms. We call them personal platforms: two-sided intermediaries whose quality is
inseparable from the composition of the communities they connect. We model an influencer as a two-sided platform connecting followers and sponsored sellers. Expansion creates network benefits but also increases cross-side mismatch. We show that the side that
is more sensitive to mismatch is optimally kept narrower. Moreover, community breadth depends on aggregate cross-side externalities, while relative prices depend on their allocation across sides. Community design and cross-subsidization are thus distinct margins,
yielding a taxonomy of personal platforms based on architecture and monetization.

title: Market Concentration, Capital Misallocation, and Asset Pricing
speaker: Thu Nguyen (Visitor from Erasmus University)
description:
Abstract:
Superstar firms, which dominate stock markets through their large size and high markups, can distort efficient capital allocation. This paper empirically studies the asset pricing implications of superstar firms through the channel of capital misallocation, measured by the cross-sectional dispersion in the marginal product of capital (MPK). Specifically, I decompose this measure into capital misallocation (1) among superstar firms, (2) among other firms, and (3) between these two groups. I find that innovations in the third component, termed the “MPK spread”, are negatively priced in the cross-section of stock returns. Stocks with negative exposure to the MPK spread outperform stocks with positive exposure by 5.44% per year. A higher MPK spread predicts lower consumption, employment, and GDP growth over the next four and eight quarters. Consistent with the Intertemporal CAPM, capital misallocation between superstar and non-superstar firms represents a state variable, and its innovations capture a macroeconomic risk factor.

title: Business Model Competition and the Supply of Privacy-preserving Apps
speaker: Doh-Shin Jeon (Toulouse School of Economics)
description:
Title:
Business Model Competition and the Supply of Privacy-preserving Apps (w/ Shota Ichihashi and Giovanni Rizzi)
Abstract:
Privacy-conscious consumers should sustain a market for subscription-funded apps that charge a fee and collect little data, yet paid apps account for only 3-5 % of apps in major app stores. We explain this puzzle with a market failure: ad-funded apps benefit from data pooled across the advertising ecosystem, whereas subscription-funded apps do not. By raising ad revenue per user in every category, these data-driven network effects strengthen ad-funded apps and tilt competition in their favor.   We model business-model competition across a continuum of app categories with endogenous entry and an equilibrium data stock determined as a fixed point. Because data raises targeting accuracy, which in turn draws more users to ad-funded apps, an exogenous increase in data is amplified in equilibrium by a data multiplier. Better targeting is pro-competitive on the intensive margin but deters privacy-preserving entry on the extensive margin.  With costless entry, better targeting always benefits consumers; with a positive entry cost, consumer surplus is single-peaked in targeting accuracy. When most apps are ad-funded, consumers benefit from limits on data combination and from digital-advertising taxes. We characterize when consent mandates can implement consumers' preferred market structure and show that a digital-advertising tax can implement it whenever laissez-faire targeting is excessive.

title: A Note on Endogenous Information Costs in Rational Inattention via Convex Duality
speaker: Stefan Behringer (Bielefeld University)
description:
Title:
A Note on Endogenous Information Costs in Rational Inattention via Convex Duality
Abstract:
The rational inattention literature employs two formulations of information costs: a hard constraint bounding mutual information by a Shannon capacity, and a soft constraint penalising mutual Information by a linear entropy penalty. We establish the structural relationship between these formulations via convex duality theory and develop its consequences. First, the hard-constraint value function, the Stratonovich/Shannon Value of Information (VoI), is the primitive object of rate distortion theory. The soft-constraint objective is its Fenchel conjugate, recoverable without parametric restriction, and the marginal cost of information is identified endogenously as the slope of the VoI; the linear entropy penalty is therefore a special case, not a maintained assumption. Second, the VoI generically depends on the full posterior distribution; it collapses to a function of posterior variance alone if and only if utility is quadratic, the prior is Gaussian, and optimal signals preserve conjugacy, three jointly necessary conditions. Third, the optimal signal Distribution takes an exponential form and generates a class of convex Risk measures; in a portfolio application, tail risk substantially amplifies information value relative to a mean-variance equivalent benchmark, a distinction that variance-based analysis cannot detect.

title: The Expected Fiscal Reaction to Monetary Policy
speaker: Bence Bardózcy (BI Norwegian Business School)
description:
Authors:
Bence Bardoczy (BI), David S. Miller (Fed Board)
Abstract.
We develop a novel high-frequency measure of the expected fiscal reaction to monetary policy and show that it implies diminished monetary policy effectiveness. Using changes around FOMC announcements in the breakeven tax rate implied by taxable Treasuries and tax-exempt municipal bond ETFs, we find that monetary tightening raises expected future taxes. This reaction has roughly halved since COVID and no longer varies with government indebtedness. We calibrate a HANK model to interpret these findings. Because all households are non-Ricardian, the interaction between the fiscal reaction and the stock of debt shapes the response of inflation to monetary policy. The weaker post-COVID reaction makes monetary tightening about half as disinflationary as it was pre-COVID, and projected higher debt levels will further erode tightening's impact.

title: Absent but Not Idle: the Social Roots of Demand for Flexible Work
speaker: Suanna Oh (Paris School of Economics)
description:
Title:
Absent but Not Idle: the Social Roots of Demand for Flexible Work (w/ Sampreet Goraya and Yogita Shamdasani)
Abstract:
High absenteeism and excess labor supply often coexist in labor markets across developing countries, creating significant challenges for both firms and workers. In this paper, we show that workers frequently experience unpredictable disruptions to their daily labor supply, hindering their ability to work regularly. Using an incentivized-choice experiment with 605 participants, we find that individuals are willing to forgo 8% of total potential earnings for day-to-day flexibility – specifically the ability to take time off without advance planning or notice. Randomly offering day-to-day flexibility leads to a 47% increase in contract compliance and a 13% increase in total earnings. Next, we document that demands from individuals’ social networks are substantial and contribute to labor supply disruptions. Consistent with this mechanism, demand for day-to-day flexibility is significantly higher when caste-based network demands are more likely to bind. Our findings provide new insight into how worker demand for flexibility shapes labor supply in developing countries.

title: Experience-based Learning, Stock Market Participation and Portfolio Choice
speaker: Richard Foltyn
description:
Abstract:
A growing body of evidence suggests that lifetime experiences play an important role in determining households' investment choices. I estimate how such experiences shape individuals' beliefs about stock returns using a long-running panel data set of elicited beliefs. I then incorporate these findings into a life cycle model and examine the extent to which they can help resolve long-standing puzzles in the literature regarding stock market participation and the fraction of financial wealth invested in risky assets. I show that experience-based learning about returns creates a positive correlation between a household's position in the wealth distribution and its optimism about future returns. The wealthy consequently increase their investment in risky assets, while participation is limited among poorer households. I find that in a reasonably calibrated quantitative model, this mechanism is able to generate limited participation and an average risky share that is close to the data.

title: Risk Prudence Premia
speaker: Fabio Girardi (Visitor from WU Vienna)
description:
Abstract:
We attribute the coskewness premium in the cross-section of equity portfolios, the negative variance risk premium, and the downward-sloping implied volatility skew to one common source, risk prudence, the aversion to downside risk. The discount factor in a minimum-divergence economy with skew-normal factor payoffs delivers this dependence through a single parameter. A decomposition into a symmetric and a downside-risk channel yields their prices of risk, estimated on U.S. characteristic-managed portfolios. The estimates have the signs the model predicts in the cross-section and in index and sector-fund options.
